headings.title: Introduction and Importance of Healthcare Waste Management
headings.content: Healthcare waste management encompasses all the waste generated within medical facilities, research centers, and laboratories. Proper handling of this waste protects healthcare personnel, patients, waste handlers, and the surrounding community from biological and chemical hazards. In many Nigerian hospitals, inadequate sorting at the bedside exposes sanitation workers to severe needlestick injuries and infectious pathogens. Establishing a rigorous classification framework is the foundational step toward mitigating environmental pollution and nosocomial disease transmission.

headings.title: General (Non-Hazardous) Healthcare Waste
headings.content: General waste constitutes the vast majority—roughly 75 to 85 percent—of all materials produced in a healthcare facility. This category includes items that have not been in contact with infectious agents, body fluids, or dangerous chemicals. Examples are office paper, cardboard, food leftovers, packaging materials, and plastic bottles from administrative or general ward areas. Because it poses no greater risk than domestic household refuse, general waste can be handled by municipal waste disposal systems without special treatment, provided it has not been cross-contaminated.

headings.title: Infectious and Pathological Waste
headings.content: Infectious waste contains pathogens in sufficient concentration or quantity to cause disease in susceptible hosts. This stream covers laboratory cultures, items soiled with blood and body fluids, and disposable patient care items like dressings and swabs. Pathological waste is a distinct sub-category consisting of human tissues, organs, body parts, and recognizable fetuses. Both types demand strict containment, typically in leak-proof bags, and undergo high-temperature incineration or autoclaving before final burial to destroy pathogenic microorganisms.

headings.title: Sharps Waste and Associated Risks
headings.content:
- **Hypodermic Needles**: Hollow-bore needles used for injections or blood draws, posing high transmission risks for bloodborne viruses.
- **Scalpels and Blades**: Surgical cutting edges that can easily penetrate standard bin liners and human skin.
- **Infusion Sets**: Tubing with attached metal needles or rigid connectors.
- **Broken Glassware**: Ampoules, slides, and capillary tubes capable of causing lacerations.

Sharps represent one of the most hazardous waste categories due to their dual capacity to cause physical trauma and transmit pathogens like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. They must be discarded immediately into puncture-resistant, leak-proof safety boxes at the point of use.

headings.title: Pharmaceutical, Chemical, and Genotoxic Waste
headings.content: This category comprises expired, unused, or contaminated chemical and drug products. Pharmaceutical waste includes vaccines, syrups, and tablets that can contaminate groundwater if improperly dumped. Chemical waste involves laboratory reagents, disinfectants, and heavy metals like mercury from broken sphygmomanometers. Genotoxic waste is highly hazardous, containing cytotoxic drugs used in cancer treatment capable of mutating DNA and causing birth defects. These substances require specialized high-temperature destruction or chemical neutralization rather than standard landfill disposal.

headings.title: Radioactive and Specialized Waste Categories
headings.content: Radioactive waste originates from nuclear medicine therapies, diagnostic tumor imaging, and clinical laboratory research using isotopes like iodine-131 or technetium-99m. It includes sealed and unsealed radiation sources, contaminated liquids, and absorbent paper. Because ionizing radiation poses severe health risks, this waste must be stored in shielded containers until its radioactivity decays to safe background levels. Specialized waste also covers pressurized gas cylinders and heavy equipment containing hazardous components, which must be managed by certified external environmental agencies.

headings.title: Color-Coding and Segregation Protocols in Nigerian Health Facilities
headings.content: Standardized color-coding is the cornerstone of effective waste segregation, ensuring that different waste streams are instantly recognizable at the point of generation. In alignment with national environmental guidelines in Nigeria, general non-hazardous waste goes into black bins, infectious and pathological items go into yellow bags or bins with biohazard symbols, and sharps are placed in rigid yellow safety boxes with puncture warnings. Chemical and pharmaceutical wastes are typically designated for brown or specially labeled containers. Strict adherence to these visual cues prevents accidental mixing and protects every tier of the healthcare delivery team.
